first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this, and the first word is 'Yes.' That's a relief, honestly. It tells me straight out that it's legal and since when, then tells them to check with the town and the Embassy before booking anything. No fuss, no slogans, and nobody treating my girls like a novelty. I'll read the lot.

journey.quote: Yes. As at November 2026, same-sex marriage in Greece is legal: Greek law allows a civil marriage between two persons of different or the same sex, and the change has been in force since 16 February 2024.
journey.reaction: Good. A plain answer with a date on it. That's what I wanted to know before I let myself get excited.

journey.quote: Before you book a venue, check the steps with the municipality where you will marry and with the Australian Embassy in Athens.
journey.reaction: Sensible order. Nobody puts money down until the paperwork side says yes. That protects our deposit before we've even paid one.

journey.quote: The law does not address foreign nationals, so the municipality where you marry sets the paperwork, and Rhodes, for one, asks for a certificate of no impediment naming your partner, translated into Greek and apostilled.
journey.reaction: I had to read that twice. Three ideas in one sentence, and 'apostilled' means nothing to me yet. It made more sense once I got to the proper section.

journey.section: Will your Greek marriage be recognised in Australia?
journey.quote: Recognised same-sex couples are treated the same as other married couples.
journey.reaction: That's the line I'll show my husband. If they marry over there, it counts here. That was his first question.

journey.section: Will your Greek marriage be recognised in Australia?
journey.quote: Your Greek marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage, but may not work as proof of a change of name, so check that with your state or territory registry of births, deaths and marriages.
journey.reaction: Useful. That's exactly the sort of thing that bites you later at the bank. I'm glad someone flagged it.

journey.quote: Every notarial service needs an appointment, Monday to Friday, 9:00am to 12:30pm, though apostille and CNI documents can be submitted by post.
journey.reaction: Very thorough, but between the CNI, the apostille, the Greek translation and the Embassy hours, I'm thinking: who actually does all this? Is it my daughter on her own, or does someone help her?

journey.section: What the law covers, and what it does not
journey.quote: The surname declaration is easy to miss in the rush of a wedding week. Ask the registrar about it when you lodge your documents.
journey.reaction: I'd never have thought of that, and they might not either. Someone has done their homework.

journey.section: Is Greece LGBT friendly for a destination wedding?
journey.quote: Racially motivated and homophobic attacks have occurred.
journey.reaction: That gave me a knot in my stomach, I won't pretend otherwise. But I'd rather read it here from the Government's advice than find out over there. Being honest about it makes me trust the rest of the page more.

journey.section: Is Greece LGBT friendly for a destination wedding?
journey.quote: Share that advice with your guests along with the itinerary.
journey.reaction: Fine for the guests, but what about the girls themselves on the day and that week? I'd like one line on how a planner keeps the celebration private and safe, not just a note to pass on.

journey.quote: In Lindos, the municipality lists St Paul's chapel platform, a tiny chapel below a cliff in the shadow of the Acropolis of Lindos, beside the turquoise water of St Paul's Bay.
journey.reaction: It sounds beautiful, but 'below a cliff' and a 'staircase' at the Town Hall make me think of steps. Mum uses a walking frame. The page never says a word about getting older guests to these places.

journey.quote: Have you hosted same-sex weddings before, and will you put that in writing?
journey.reaction: Yes. In writing. I don't want anyone on the day looking at my daughter and her partner as if they're a problem. That question alone is worth forwarding.

journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is a single point of contact who plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments around your civil ceremony, works in your time zone and quotes in AUD, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins
journey.reaction: One person, our time zone, Australian dollars, the fee in writing first. That's what I need to hear before I contribute anything.

journey.section: Legal ceremony, symbolic celebration or both
journey.quote: Some couples keep the civil ceremony small, with the two witnesses and close family, and hold the larger celebration that evening or the next day.
journey.reaction: That's lovely, and it suits us. A quiet legal bit with family, then the party. I can picture it.

journey.section: Plan your Greece wedding with Wedded Concierge
journey.quote: The registrar settles the marriage. Everything around it, from the island and the venue to your guests' rooms and the long dinner after, is ours to plan.
journey.reaction: Nicely put, and it's clear who does what. I'd still want a phone call with a real person before a cent goes anywhere.

unanswered_questions: If we book through Wedded Concierge, who actually handles the CNI, apostille and Greek translation: my daughter, the venue or the Wedded Advisor?
Are the town hall, the chapel below the cliff and the beach locations reachable for someone with a walking frame, or is it steps and sand?
How does a planner keep the ceremony and celebration private and safe for a same-sex couple, given the Smartraveller warning?
What travel and medical insurance should older relatives have for a wedding in Greece?
Is the deposit protected, and who reads a contract written in Greek and in euros?
Who do I ring if something goes wrong at 2am Greek time?
Is the first step a phone call with a real person, before anything is booked or paid?

turn_offs_found.quote: The law does not address foreign nationals, so the municipality where you marry sets the paperwork, and Rhodes, for one, asks for a certificate of no impediment naming your partner, translated into Greek and apostilled.
turn_offs_found.why: It's meant to be a quick takeaway but it crams the law, the town, Rhodes, the certificate, translation and apostille into one line. On the iPad I lost the thread and had to go back. A takeaway should be the easy bit.

turn_offs_found.quote: Every notarial service needs an appointment, Monday to Friday, 9:00am to 12:30pm, though apostille and CNI documents can be submitted by post. Apostilled documents and CNIs are ready for collection within two working days unless same-day collection is arranged in advance, or they can be returned by mail. A fee applies.
turn_offs_found.why: It's a solid block of hours, days, post and collection rules. Fine to have, but it reads like a government form and I started to glaze over. Short points would let me print it for my husband.

would_share_with: My husband, with the recognition section ('treated the same as other married couples') and the Wedded Advisor paragraph (AUD, fee in writing)
My daughter and her partner, with the surname declaration point and the venue questions list
My sister, who will travel with Mum, once the page says something about access to the ceremony spots

cta_reaction.quote: One Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you as a single point of contact, anywhere in the world, and confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
cta_reaction.why: It ticks my boxes: one person, AUD, the fee and inclusions in writing. I'd click once the girls have checked the paperwork with the town, and I'd want to know a real person rings us first and helps with the Greek documents, getting Mum around and keeping the day safe and private.

top_3_changes: In 'What Australians arrange' or the Wedded Advisor paragraph, add one plain sentence on who helps with the CNI, apostille and Greek translation in practice, so a parent isn't left thinking the couple does it all alone.

Near 'a tiny chapel below a cliff' and the Town Hall staircase, add one line that ceremony spots can mean steps, sand or uneven paths, and that access for older guests is worth confirming with the municipality and venue before you commit. Mobility is never mentioned.

Split the takeaway 'The law does not address foreign nationals, so the municipality where you marry sets the paperwork, and Rhodes, for one...' into two short sentences, and turn the Embassy hours paragraph into short points. Both are hard going on an iPad.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Margaret (funding parent of a same-sex couple, practical, reads top to bottom on an iPad, sent the link by her daughter)
No invented brand facts; missing business details listed as unanswered questions
HTML comments, image slots and VERIFY markers treated as invisible
Deferred business details (deposits, contracts, 2am contact, call first) and transfers not raised as must-fix; absent prices, named venues and sourcing not raised as problems, per orchestrator
Journey types limited to the allowed enum; every turn-off has a why

open_questions.question: Mobility for older guests (Town Hall staircase, chapel below a cliff, beaches) is never mentioned, this persona's top practical worry: should-fix? Who helps with the CNI, apostille and translation is a medium gap. The Smartraveller safety paragraph is honest and builds trust, but a parent wants one line on how the celebration is kept private and safe. Two dense paragraphs (a takeaway bullet and the Embassy hours) are readability turn-offs. Deposits, contract language, 2am contact and call-first are deferred business details.

assumptions: Margaret's daughter is one half of the couple and sent the link; Margaret is supportive and reads the whole article on an iPad, and her own mother uses a walking frame (per voice samples).
Prices and named venues are deliberately absent and the brand does not discuss sourcing, so none were raised.
